headline: Cuba reconnects a grid still short two gigawatts
deck: National system interlinked west to east after successive collapses, yet available generation remains more than two gigawatts below peak demand.
body: The national system was interconnected from Pinar del Río to Holguín while work continued in the east.[E1] This restoration followed successive total collapses that had left the island dark. Operators rebuilt transmission links across the western and central provinces before turning to the east. The grid was once again operating as a single system.

Reconnection is not the same as adequate supply. UNE forecast 1,035 MW available against 3,200 MW demand and a 2,195 MW peak impact.[E2] Those figures reveal a deficit of more than two gigawatts at the evening peak. The arithmetic of shortfall has not changed simply because the system is once again synchronised.

Three distinct layers of failure must be kept separate. The first is the total cascade that took the entire system offline. At 22:43 a total disconnection of the National Electroenergetic System occurred.[E3] No public technical explanation has yet been issued for the precise initiating event.

The second is the re-collapse while restoration was under way. A frequency oscillation during restoration produced another total disconnection.[E4] That disruption erased the day’s progress. Operators were forced to begin the black-start sequence again.

The third and decisive layer is structural. Ten thermoelectric units were out of service before the national collapses.[E5] These offline plants represent a large share of thermal capacity. Their absence, not the momentary trips, produces the persistent two-gigawatt peak shortfall.

Each successive reconnection demonstrates operational resilience under extreme constraint. Incremental returns of units gradually close portions of the gap. Those returns are real and measurable. They have not, however, altered the order of magnitude of the shortfall that UNE itself publishes.

Until generation capacity moves materially closer to peak demand, electrical reconnection will continue to coexist with multi-hour blackouts. The engineering facts of unit availability and demand forecasts stand clear. The grid is once again one system. It remains two gigawatts short of being an adequate one.
